summary: This best current practice document describes the reservation of Autonomous System Numbers for private use and gives operational guidance. It enlarges the private use space by documenting a second, larger reserved range. It updates RFC 1930 by replacing Section 10.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6996 reserves two ranges of Autonomous System Numbers (ASNs) for private use, one small and one very large. It matters because networks can number themselves without registered numbers, as long as they strip those numbers out before routes reach the global Internet.

subtitle: Reserves a second, much larger block of AS numbers for networks that do not need globally unique ones.

tldr.problem: The original block of 1023 private AS numbers was too small for new BGP uses such as data center networks, and it cannot be renumbered because private numbers are not registered.
tldr.mechanism: IANA keeps the range 64512 - 65534 from the 16-bit registry and reserves a second, larger range, 4200000000 - 4294967294, from the 32-bit registry.
tldr.outcome: Operators get far more private AS numbers, but private ASNs MUST be removed from AS paths before routes are advertised to the global Internet.

today: RFC 6996 is a Best Current Practice and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 1930 by replacing Section 10 of that document.

sections.title: Why a Bigger Private Range
sections.content:
The original IANA reservation of Autonomous System Numbers (ASNs) for Private Use was a block of 1023 ASNs, also documented by the IETF in Section 10 of RFC 1930. Since that range was reserved, the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) has seen deployment in new application domains, such as data center networks, which require a larger Private Use AS space.

Since the introduction of four-octet AS number space in RFC 6793, the total size of ASN space has increased dramatically, so a larger subset of the space is available to network operators for these Private Use cases. The existing range is widely deployed and cannot be renumbered, because these ASNs, by definition, are not registered. The RFC therefore documents the existing reservation while introducing a second, larger range.
sections.plainLanguage: The old private range had only 1023 numbers and cannot be changed, because private numbers are not registered anywhere. This RFC keeps the old range and adds a much bigger one.

sections.title: The Two Private Use Ranges
sections.content:
Two ranges of ASNs are reserved: the first is part of the original 16-bit Autonomous System range defined in RFC 1930, and the second is a larger range out of the four-octet AS number space. Section 5 of the RFC records the reservations in the IANA "Autonomous System (AS) Numbers" registry.

IANA has reserved, for Private Use, a contiguous block of 1023 Autonomous System numbers from the 16-bit registry, namely 64512 - 65534 inclusive. IANA has also reserved a contiguous block of 94,967,295 Autonomous System numbers from the 32-bit registry, namely 4200000000 - 4294967294 inclusive.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two private ranges: 64512 to 65534 in the old numbering, and 4200000000 to 4294967294 in the new four-octet numbering.

sections.title: Operational Rules
sections.content:
If Private Use ASNs are used and prefixes originate from these ASNs, the Private Use ASNs MUST be removed from AS path attributes, including AS4_PATH if a four-octet AS number space is used, before being advertised to the global Internet. Normal AS path filtering MAY also be used to prevent prefixes originating from Private Use ASNs from being advertised to the global Internet.

Operators SHOULD ensure that all External Border Gateway Protocol (EBGP) speakers support the four-octet extensions and that features recognizing Private Use ASNs have been updated to recognize both ranges before the newer, numerically higher range is used. Some existing implementations do not remove Private Use ASNs from the AS_PATH when the path contains a mixture of private and non-private ASNs; if they do not know the new range, they will likely cease to remove Private Use ASNs from either path attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: Private numbers must be taken out of the path before a route is shared with the wider Internet. The equipment doing that must know about the new range first, or it may stop stripping them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Private Use ASNs do not raise any unique security concerns. Loss of connectivity might result from their inappropriate use outside a single organization, since they are not globally unique, and that loss is limited to the organization using them inappropriately or without following the operational rules.

Identification of the originator of a route with a Private Use ASN in the AS path has to be done by tracking the route back to the neighboring globally unique AS in the path, or by inspecting other attributes. General BGP security considerations are discussed in RFC 4271 and RFC 4272.
sections.plainLanguage: Misusing a private number mainly breaks your own network. Finding who originated such a route means following it back to the nearest registered network.
